title: Why X/Γ is an orbifold when Γ has torsion
question: Let X=G/K be the contractible symmetric space of a connected semisimple Lie group with finite center and let \Gamma< G be a uniform lattice that contains an involution. Why does the quotient X/\Gamma fail to be a manifold, and how can one describe the local orbifold chart near the image of a fixed point of that involution?
answer: If \Gamma is torsion-free then its action on X is free and properly discontinuous, so the quotient X/\Gamma is a manifold and in fact aspherical. When \Gamma contains torsion, pick x\in X fixed by an element \gamma\in\Gamma of finite order. The stabilizer \Gamma_x is finite (because G acts properly on X), and the linear isotropy representation identifies \Gamma_x with a finite subgroup of O(T_xX). Thus the action fails to be free precisely on the fixed-point set X^{\gamma}, and the quotient is modelled on the linear slice T_xX/\Gamma_x rather than T_xX.\n\nThe slice theorem provides a \Gamma_x-invariant neighborhood U of x such that the \Gamma-saturation \Gamma\cdot U projects homeomorphically onto (U/\Gamma_x)\subset X/\Gamma. Because \Gamma_x is finite, U/\Gamma_x is a classical orbifold chart. Therefore X/\Gamma is an orbifold whose singular locus corresponds to the images of fixed-point sets of torsion elements, and only after passing to a torsion-free finite-index subgroup does one recover a genuine manifold quotient.
